I was recently watching/listening to [a video essay by OliSUNvia](https://youtu.be/NJZ5YNrXMpE) (which you should totally watch/listen to also because she talks about some really interesting stuff) on how everything has become a form of entertainment these days. Most of what she says won’t be new information to anyone listening, but deeply thinking about why/how we got to this point gives you a lot to chew on. There’s tons of ideas worth talking about in the video, but as she was making her points, one very clear question bubbled to the surface. **Should learning be entertaining?** This could mean the kind of learning we do in our daily life. Useful information like news, lifestyle tips, or hearing your family history come to mind. But what stood out to me were the questions I formed when thinking about formal learning like at a school or from an informal teacher. Is it the teacher’s job to be entertaining? What does it take to keep someone’s attention while we teach them? If we get bored while we are listening, does that mean the content being heard or taught isn’t worth being listened to?

I tutor occasionally (much more when I was in college) and I’ve also been teaching Sunday school for 9th and 10th graders recently so for me, the answers to these questions are extremely relevant. My initial thought was “of course learning should be kind of fun”. That’s what gets the learner invested. We help kids learn by letting them do activities like coloring or singing songs. We help adolescents learn by using videos or talking about relevant topics. We help adults learn by using a mixture of visuals and discussion (and also by making them pay for it). But the more I think about those examples, I think what I’m actually talking about here isn’t necessarily “entertainment”, though it can be. It’s _engagement._ One of the best way to learn something is to be engaged with what you’re learning. That could be through related activities, questions, or visuals. When you’re first starting to learn how to code, there’s a phase we call “tutorial hell”. It’s when you keep watching tutorials on some concept and taking courses, but you’ve yet to actually go and code up a project using what you’ve learned. The best way to learn in that instance is to start up a project, work until you fail, learn what’s missing, and repeat. That’s an example of being engaged. And for that reason, some programming courses include hands on exercises and projects that you complete mid lesson. But I believe that’s different from just being entertained in a way that doesn’t elevate or help teach the content in any meaningful way. Most of the Sunday school lessons that I teach come with notes and guides, including an activity for the students to start the class off. I do not do the activities. Primarily because those activities are often loosely connected to the lesson. But also because I don’t think any 9th & 10th graders would want to take turns trying to fit children’s clothes over one another (yes that was a real suggested activity). Now those kind of fun(?) activities have their place, but is that really the best way to begin teaching students? I’ve also noticed in my class that occasionally a student pulls out their phone and will scroll or watch something real quick. I’m far from a perfect or even proficient teacher, but does this happen because they aren’t being engaged or because they aren’t being entertained? Considering the fact that the class is more about open conversation and discussion than reading slides, I lean toward the latter. But then that raises the question I mentioned before. Is it the teacher’s job to entertain students? Should we be trying to compete for attention with a super computer that can instantly load any game, video, or image? Should people be drawn to what we have to teach based solely on how entertaining we are? I have to believe that’s not it chief. That kind of mentality is how you get a monster truck show at a church men’s conference (yes that is also real).

I don’t really know what the best way to go about addressing this issue is, at a societal level or even at a personal one in my own teaching. It’s hard to just overcome distractions by sheer power of will. I’ve stopped like three times to check my phone even in the middle of writing this short post. Many teachers don’t try to compete with the smartphone; they just remove the distraction by taking the phone. That’s probably the easiest and most effective method, though it won’t earn you any brownie points with your students. Other teachers try to compete by adding surprises to the lesson or a longer video, but you can’t do that every lesson. Eventually you’ll have to sacrifice meaningful learning to keep up. The only reasonable way forward to me at the moment is to just do your best to make the content you’re teaching relevant to your students and show how they might actually use what they’ve learned. At least that way, a student motivated to learn is helping you fight their distraction rather than you dealing with a bored student who embraces it.
